result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_havel_hakimi_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a graph with a given degree sequence, built deterministically by the Havel-Hakimi ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L10629-L10733){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_havel_hakimi_graph( degree_sequence, type=None, label=True, rel=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} algorithm. ![Havel-Hakimi graph](/assets/graphs/add-havel-hakimi-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three Havel-Hakimi graphs on five nodes, each node's requested degree in a pill: 3, 2, 2, 2, 1; 3, 3, 2, 2, 2; and 4, 3, 3, 2, 2. The construction is deterministic, joining the node with the most degree left to the next-highest nodes, and every node ends with exactly the degree in its pill, using 5, 6, and 7 edges." width="100%"} Creates one node per entry of `degree_sequence`, and node `i` gets exactly `degree_sequence[i]` neighbors, with no self-loops or parallel edges. The Havel-Hakimi algorithm repeatedly takes the node with the largest remaining degree `d` and joins it to the `d` nodes with the next-largest remaining degrees. It succeeds exactly when the sequence is graphical (some simple graph has these degrees), which is checked first with the Erdős-Gallai test. There is no randomness: the same sequence always gives the same graph. Because high-degree nodes are joined first, they tend to link to each other, so the result is strongly assortative. For a random graph with the same degrees, see `add_random_degree_sequence_graph()` (simple) or `configuration_model()` (with self-loops and parallel edges). The process follows NetworkX's `havel_hakimi_graph()` and gives the same edges. NetworkX numbers only the nodes of nonzero degree, though, so when the sequence contains zeros its node `i` may not have degree `degree_sequence[i]`; here it always does. In a directed graph every edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Havel-Hakimi graphs are useful for: - checking that a degree sequence can be realized, and getting one realization - a deterministic, maximally assortative starting point for degree-preserving rewiring (see `double_edge_swap()`) - test graphs with exactly prescribed degrees ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [degree_sequence]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Degree of each new node, as a list of non-negative integers. The sum must be even. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `degree_sequence=` contains a negative entry or is not graphical. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Each node gets the degree at its position in the sequence: ::: {#10340894 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_havel_hakimi_graph([3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1]) [graph.get_degree(v) for v in sorted(graph.get_node_ids())] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1] ``` ::: ::: The highest-degree nodes are joined to each other first: ::: {#8b48ce46 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_edges_str_repr() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['1--2', '1--3', '1--4', '2--3', '2--4', '5--6'] ``` ::: ::: A sequence with no simple realization is rejected. Two nodes of degree three would each need three distinct neighbors among only three others, two of which have degree one: ::: {#e2d53a2d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} try: ec.Graph().add_havel_hakimi_graph([3, 3, 1, 1]) except ValueError as err: print(err) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` degree_sequence is not graphical: no simple graph has these degrees ``` ::: :::
